claim: The highest-impact science pairs mostly conventional prior work with a tail of unusual combinations; hit rate 9.11 per 100 vs 5 per 100 background.
quote: Papers with "high median conventionality" and "high tail novelty" display a hit rate of 9.11 out of 100 papers, or nearly twice the background rate of 5 out of 100 papers.
title: Atypical combinations and scientific impact
transfer: Idea generator: keep most of the answer on well-known ground and insert one or two distant links, instead of going fully novel.

claim: Novelty without a conventional base does not pay: low conventionality with high tail novelty had hit rate 5.33 per 100 (near background 5); low on both was 2.05.
quote: Finally, papers low on both dimensions have hit rates of just 2.05 out of 100.
title: Atypical combinations and scientific impact
transfer: Forced divergence alone (our NoveltyBench schema) is not enough for quality. Anchor in a conventional core and judge the odd part.

claim: Most papers are highly conventional; a median combination below chance is rare (3.54% in the 1980s), yet about 40% of papers have some unusual tail combinations.
quote: papers with a median z-score below zero are rare. In the 1980s only 3.54% of papers had this feature
title: Atypical combinations and scientific impact
transfer: An LLM default is the conventional mode. The step to add is a deliberate small tail of distant links.

claim: TEAM ONLY: teams are 37.7% more likely than solo authors to insert novel combinations into familiar knowledge.
quote: teams are 37.7% more likely than solo authors to insert
title: Atypical combinations and scientific impact
transfer: Team-level result. Single-agent analog is several personas from different domains, but samples from one model are correlated, so expect less.

claim: Papers making many distant first-time journal combinations get 12.04% more citations and 14.90% higher citation dispersion than non-novel ones.
quote: highly novel papers receive 12.04% more citations.
title: Bias against novelty in science (working paper; later Research Policy 2017)
n: all WoS articles of 2001, 251 subject categories
transfer: Novel ideas are high variance. Generate many, expect most to fail, keep an objective pruner.

claim: Novel papers sit in both tails: odds of top-10% cited are 16.80% higher and odds of lowest-10% cited 16.76% higher than for non-novel papers.
quote: the odds of being the top 10% cited versus being the middle 80% cited are 16.80% higher for highly novel than non-novel papers.
title: Bias against novelty in science (working paper; later Research Policy 2017)
n: all WoS articles of 2001, 251 subject categories
transfer: A novel idea's quality is bimodal. Do not trust a quick self-rating, use an external check.

claim: Delayed recognition: novel papers are less likely to be top-cited in a short window and tend to appear in lower-impact-factor journals.
quote: novel papers are less likely to be top cited when using a short time window
title: Bias against novelty in science (working paper; later Research Policy 2017)
n: all WoS articles of 2001, 251 subject categories
transfer: Early-recognition problem: a fast score undervalues novel candidates. Give novel options a longer test before dropping them.

claim: Only 11% of papers make any new journal combination; of those 55% make exactly one and 7% make more than five.
title: Bias against novelty in science (working paper; later Research Policy 2017)
n: all WoS articles of 2001, 251 subject categories
transfer: Base rate: genuine recombination is rare, so a schema that always demands it will mostly yield unfit ideas.

claim: New component combinations give lower average usefulness but higher variance, so both failure and breakthrough come from unfamiliar search.
quote: Experimentation with new components and new combinations leads to less useful inventions on average, but it also implies an increase in the variability that can result in both failure and breakthrough.
title: Recombinant uncertainty in technological search
n: US patent citation data (n not read)
transfer: Explains our split result: divergence pays on open tasks (many tries, a pruner) and costs on single-answer tasks where the mean matters.

claim: Combination familiarity raised expected citations about 10-11% in the model, but familiarity did not reduce outcome uncertainty as predicted.
quote: While the results support Hypothesis 1, they do not support Hypothesis 2, that component learning decreases the uncertainty of invention.
title: Recombinant uncertainty in technological search
n: US patent citation data (n not read)
transfer: Learning from a domain lifts the average, not breakthrough odds. A lessons ledger helps mean quality only.

claim: In about 6.4 million biomedical and chemistry papers (1934-2008) most work follows tradition; innovative links are less often published but better cited when published.
title: Tradition and innovation in scientists' research strategies
transfer: Innovation is a gamble with a modest mean payoff. Confirm with a second source: I read press coverage only (journal page returned 403).

claim: Prize winners show more innovative moves in their research portfolio, suggesting rare bets drive top impact.
title: Tradition and innovation in scientists' research strategies
transfer: Portfolio view: keep a small share of tries as long-shot bets, the rest safe. Press coverage only.

claim: March (1991): exploration and exploitation compete for scarce resources; organisations under-invest in exploration because exploitation returns are surer and sooner.
title: Exploration and exploitation in organizational learning
transfer: Explicit explore/exploit budget; start exploring at impasse. ORGANISATION-level model, so the single-agent use is by analogy. Summary seen, primary not opened.

claim: A 2018 review of the research inspired by March (1991) calls for microfoundations of exploration and exploitation, i.e. individual-level behaviour.
title: Revisiting James March (1991): whither exploration and exploitation?
transfer: The individual-level version is under-studied, so evidence for one agent here is thin.

claim: Problem-finding art students (explored objects longer, shaped the problem while working) produced work judged better and gained more recognition years later.
quote: Those with a discovery orientation toward their work, rather than an already established idea of what they would do, generally produced works of art that were judged by experts to be better than the rest.
title: The creative vision: a longitudinal study of problem finding in art
n: aspiring artists, Art Institute of Chicago (n not read)
transfer: Open-ended tasks: spend an early phase exploring and reframing before committing. Not for single-answer puzzles. Secondary account; effect size unknown.

claim: Per a review, intelligence did not correlate with studio performance or later professional success in the artist study.
title: The creative vision
transfer: Weak: process, not raw ability, may drive the creative gain. Low confidence, review not opened.

claim: Smaller teams introduce new ideas and are later cited as disruptive; larger teams extend existing work. 65 million works, 1954-2014.
quote: Differences in topic and research design account for a small part of the relationship between team size and disruption; most of the effect occurs at the level of the individual, as people move between smaller and larger teams.
title: Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology
transfer: TEAM ONLY mostly. The individual-level part hints a lean-context divergent call vs a big-context develop call.

claim: Small-team work searches deeper into the past; large-team work builds on recent, popular developments.
quote: contributions by smaller teams search more deeply into the past
title: Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology
transfer: Retrieval step: pull older, distant sources, not the most popular recent pattern. LLMs default to popular patterns.

claim: Escalation of commitment is a robust, costly error: sunk costs and other determinants keep decision makers on losing paths.
quote: The topic of escalation of commitment has intrigued the organizational sciences for over 35 years.
title: Cleaning up the Big Muddy: a meta-analytic review of the determinants of escalation of commitment
n: over 160 studies (per a citing paper; table not read)
transfer: Why ideas that should die survive: set a kill rule in advance and judge each branch as if new, ignoring tokens already spent.
